newsitem.title: USA: Boston $700mln convention center bill emerges anew.
newsitem.headline: Boston $700mln convention center bill emerges anew.

text.p: A much-altered convention center bill emerged from a new House committee charged with looking at capital projects to assure they are economically feasible and affordable, State House News Service reported.

The House Long-Term Debt and Capital Spending Committee made major changes in the bill on Tuesday that had moved from the State Administration Committee a day earlier, and that had represented a merger of two bills filed by Gov. William F. Weld to spur economic development.
Dumped from the legislation paving the way for a new $700 million convention center in Boston were funds for planned capital projects in Lenox, Fall River and Southeastern Massachusetts.
Retained was money for major projects in Springfield and Worcester but those two cities would join Boston and Cambridge in hiking their hotel/motel excise taxes by 2.5 percent.
Also stricken from the legislation was a call that voters in the affected areas must first approve that tax hike, as Weld has insisted.
Rep. Patricia Walrath, who chairs the panel, said additional fees would be imposed to insure a revenue stream sufficient to support the projects.

They include a $10 surcharge on car rentals in Boston, a $1 add-on to the price of tickets for sightseeing tours within 15 miles of the Boston and Worcester facilities, and a $1 surcharge for parking at the facilities in Boston, Springfield and Worcester.
Walrath reasoned that since Springfield and Worcester are benefiting under the bill, they should be required to protect the revenue stream needed to pay for the projects.

Like its predecessors, the new bill relies on the hotel/motel tax hike, along with the earmarking of sales tax revenues around Boston's new convention center and a $125 million commitment from the city of Boston, to support the revenue bonds that would be used to finance the projects.
"We really are not in a position to do general obligation stuff," Walrath said, alluding to the competition for capital funds under a $900-million-a-year ceiling on long-term borrowing.

There are also stipulations, or conditions in the bill. The Boston City Council and mayor must appropriate "no less than $125 million" for site acquisition and preparation, and hotel developers must "present loan commitment letters from recognized lenders."

BankBoston, leading a small group of Boston-based businesses, is offering to help close the financing gap for the proposed $700 million convention center in exchange for naming rights, The Boston Globe reported on Wednesday.

It is not clear if BankBoston's offer of $20 million will be accepted. Boston Mayor Thomas Menino says the city can afford only $130 million, but House Speaker Thomas Finneran wants Boston to come up with $205 million for the project.
The next stop for the convention center bill is the House Ways and Means Committee. Speaker Finneran said House floor debate on the measure will be scheduled for July 14th.
